summary: The document provides a high-level functional overview of a Hospital Management System (HMS), listing core modules (EMR, Billing, Pharmacy, etc.) and a generic tech stack (React, FastAPI, PostgreSQL). However, it lacks specific technical specifications, data models, API contracts, and critical healthcare compliance details (HIPAA/GDPR/HL7 FHIR). It reads as a project brief rather than a detailed software requirements specification (SRS) or architectural design document.

risk_factors.title: Lack of Specific PHI Encryption Standards
risk_factors.description: The document mentions 'password encryption' and 'privacy of medical information' but does not specify AES-256 for data at rest or TLS 1.2+ for data in transit, which are mandatory for HIPAA compliance regarding Protected Health Information (PHI).
risk_factors.mitigation: Explicitly define cryptographic standards: AES-256-GCM for PHI at rest, TLS 1.3 for all API communications, and key management strategy (e.g., AWS KMS or HashiCorp Vault).

risk_factors.title: Missing Interoperability Standards (HL7 FHIR/DICOM)
risk_factors.description: The document lists 'electronic medical records' and 'laboratory test reports' but fails to mention HL7 FHIR or DICOM standards. This will prevent interoperability with other healthcare systems, imaging devices, and labs, violating modern healthcare integration requirements.
risk_factors.mitigation: Specify that the EMR module must expose HL7 FHIR R4 resources (Patient, Observation, MedicationRequest) and support DICOM for imaging data ingestion and storage.

risk_factors.title: Ambiguous Audit Trail Immutability
risk_factors.description: The document mentions 'audit logs' and 'auditability' but does not specify immutability. In healthcare, audit trails must be tamper-proof to satisfy HIPAA Security Rule and GDPR accountability principles.
risk_factors.mitigation: Define that audit logs must be written to an append-only storage system (e.g., WORM storage or blockchain-based ledger) and that no user, including Admins, can delete or modify audit entries.

risk_factors.title: Generic Database Choice Without Partitioning Strategy
risk_factors.description: The document suggests 'PostgreSQL/MySQL' without addressing data partitioning for PHI. Storing all data in a single monolithic database increases the risk of data leakage and complicates GDPR 'Right to Erasure' requests.
risk_factors.mitigation: Specify a data partitioning strategy where PHI is stored in a separate, highly secured schema or database instance, isolated from non-PHI operational data.

risk_factors.mitigation: Define strict NFRs: RTO < 1 hour and RPO < 5 minutes, with automated failover mechanisms and regular disaster recovery drills.

ai_recommendations: Integrate HL7 FHIR R4 standards into the EMR and Laboratory modules to ensure interoperability with other healthcare systems and devices.
Implement AES-256 encryption for all PHI at rest and TLS 1.3 for data in transit, with a robust key management strategy using a dedicated KMS.
Define and enforce an immutable audit trail for all access to PHI, ensuring that logs cannot be modified or deleted by any user, including administrators.
Specify strict RTO (< 1 hour) and RPO (< 5 minutes) benchmarks and implement automated failover and backup mechanisms to meet these targets.
Create a detailed RBAC matrix that explicitly defines data visibility and permissions for each role, ensuring that sensitive clinical data is not accessible to non-clinical staff.
